Good morning, distinguished delegates. I declare open our meeting of the Legal Subcommittee of the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space. I hope that you have all had a good weekend and that we are ready and prepared to successfully conclude our work this week in a couple of days. This morning, as I said last Friday, we will begin our consideration of agenda item 4, general exchange of views, then we will continue and conclude our consideration of agenda item 12, general exchange of views on the legal aspects of space traffic management. Then we will begin and hopefully conclude our consideration of agenda item 13 and then we will adjourn the plenary so that the working group on legal aspects of space resource activities can hold its third meeting. Having mentioned all of this, I would now begin with the list of speakers that we have for agenda item four, and I give the floor to the delegation of Poland.

Thank you, Chair. Mr. Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, At the outset, I would like to congratulate you, Mr. Chair, on your election. On behalf of the Polish delegation, I wish you every success in leading the 65th session of the Legal Subcommittee. We also thank former Chair, Mr. Ripoll Carrulla, for successfully guiding us through the last two sessions. I would like also to express our appreciation to Ms. Arty Holamini, Director of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, and the entire Secretariat for their outstanding work in preparing and managing the current session. Poland fully aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, inter alia with the call to respect international law, and we share the strong condemnation of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. Mr. Chair, distinguished delegates, I am pleased to announce that on 13 February 2026, the Polish Parliament adopted the Act on Space Activities, marking a significant step in aligning Poland's national legal framework with the international obligations arising from the United Nations space treaties. The new Space Act establishes a coherent set of rules for the functioning of the space sector, simultaneously strengthening national security and protecting the financial interests of the Polish State. Specifically, this new piece of legislation provides a framework for both the evaluation of licence applications and the subsequent supervision of operators. Accordingly, operators are required to consider the long term sustainable use of outer space for peaceful purposes and to eliminate or minimise negative impacts on the natural environment of Earth or outer space, including preventing the formation of space debris. Let me emphasise that the Polish Parliament, while developing the Space Act took into consideration the internationally agreed legal framework, including the provisions of guidelines for the long term sustainability of outer space activities. Furthermore, the Act establishes the national register of space objects. Another significant element is the set of provisions governing liability for damage caused by space objects. Additionally, the Act enhances the security of citizens and the state by creating a legal regime for the operation of the national satellite information system and the space security system, both being of utmost importance for crisis management and national security in terms of threats to public safety, environment and infrastructure. Mr. Chair, The foreseeable human exploration of the Moon and increasing frequency of lunar missions will heighten the risk of harmful impact on lunar environment and heritage lunar sites. Therefore, we welcome progress made by the Action Team on Lunar Activities Consultations and advocate for preservation of human heritage on the Moon in the interest of all mankind and future generations. We also look forward to an agreement on the objectives, venue, organisation and funding of the UniSpace4 conference. Finally, I would like to announce that Poland was selected to organise the 78th International Astronautical Congress, which will be held in Poznan, Poland, from 27 September to 1 October 2027. Therefore, let me take this opportunity to cordially invite you to this important event on the topic One space, shared future'. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the delegation of Poland for that statement, which is the last Member State that I have on my list. I now give the floor to observers, beginning with the Lunar Policy Platform Foundation.

Thank you very much, Chair.

I am delighted to congratulate you on your election as Chair of the Legal Subcommittee and would like to assure you of our full support. We also wish to sincerely thank Professor Santiago Ripoll from Spain for guiding the Subcommittee over the past two years, as well as the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs for the excellent organization of this year's meetings despite the many challenges of the liquidity crisis. The Lunar Policy Platform or LPP is an expert, neutral, global, non-governmental organization specializing in lunar policy. Our mission is to help create and maintain a conducive policy environment enabling the peaceful, safe and sustainable exploration and use of the Moon for the benefit of all humanity. Our work covers the entire value chain of policy, development, implementation and education and is designed to support the leading work of COPUOS as the multilateral body in charge of space governance. In policy development, with gratitude to our former funder and trusted partner, the Open Lunar Foundation, last year we produced three groundbreaking reports advancing lunar policy worldwide. First, we developed a lunar information sharing one-on-one to clarify common ground between all actors on the core elements of lunar information sharing and foster the development of guiding principles and streamline practices. Second, we developed a guide to lunar science and ethics to identify scientific, cultural, and ethical interest in lunar activities, gather views on their regard, and suggest foundational principles and procedures for a balanced approach. Third and final, we released the second edition of our lunar policy snapshot, a unique document capturing lunar developments, outlining stakeholder views, analyzing the policy ecosystems, and forecasting key implications for the future. In policy education, we partnered with research institutions and space agencies worldwide to organize events for capacity building and awareness raising. Together with the Korea Aerospace Research Institute, KARI, and with the kind support of the Korea Aerospace Administration, KASA, we co-hosted an online series of expert seminars to raise awareness and develop a better understanding of key issues for safe and sustainable lunar activities. The series featured nearly 300 participants from over 30 countries, fostering capacity building worldwide. Together with the Royal Astronomical Society and in partnership with the UK Space Agency, we hosted the first Lunar Community Building Workshop in London. This intimate event featured 50 participants across the UK space sector and fostered open discussions to identify synergies and promote cooperation. After becoming fully independent and establishing our own legal entities, in 2026 we're scaling up our impact in collaboration with new partners worldwide. In policy development, we're conducting consultations on the legal and policy aspects of lunar nuclear reactors. Over 20 organizations participated so far and we're welcoming initial contributions until April 30. Further information is provided in CRP number six. In policy education, we are collaborating with partners across four continents to organizing impactful events for a shared future in space. Last month, on March 9, together with the University of Tokyo, we co-hosted the first Space Law and Policy Symposium on Space Resource Activities of Japan. This event brought together 150 participants from the Japanese space community, fostering insightful discussions on coordination and cooperation. Next month on May 20, together with IAA, we will co-host the Global Leaders Space Exploration Forum, convening a curated group of space agencies, industry leaders, and policy officials to foster strategic alignment and impactful action in Washington, DC. We invite all delegations interested in our activities to find us during the session. We will be delighted to answer any questions, exchange views, and explore opportunities to collaborate. Thank you very much for your kind attention.
I thank The LPP for that statement and now I give the floor to the Square Kilometre Array Observatory.

Chair, distinguished delegates, on behalf of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, SKAO, I'm pleased to report the outcomes of the United Nations and SKAO workshop on dark and quiet skies for science and society held from the 9th to the 11th of December 2025 here in Vienna and online. A staggering 511 people representing 86 countries registered for the event, 59% of which came from developing states. This workshop was jointly organised with ANUSA and forms part of our shared efforts to address the growing challenges posed by large satellite constellations to both optical and radio astronomy. The event formed part of the broader yearly consideration by the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee of the agenda item, Dark and Quiet Skies, Astronomy and Large Constellations, addressing emerging issues and challenges, which will remain on the STSC agenda until 2029. The workshop brought together scientists, the satellite industry, space agencies, academia, regulators, policymakers, lawyers, and the diplomatic community. The substance and contributions of this event are captured comprehensively in the official United Nations report, reference A/AC.0105/1348, which provides detailed summaries of the objectives, discussions and recommendations emerging from the workshop. The report highlights three important areas of progress. First, the participants examined advances made in prediction and measurement tools designed to better assess and mitigate the impacts of satellite constellations. This included updates on tools enabling more accurate forecasting of optical streaks and radio interference, as well as new opportunities for observatories and satellite operators to collaborate on data sharing and operational coordination. Secondly, the workshop reviewed the regulatory approaches and policies developed in different countries, helping to identify opportunities for more consistent, internationally aligned mitigation frameworks. These examples provide a valuable foundation for future international dialogue on the legal and policy aspects of protecting dark and quiet skies. Thirdly, the report highlights the essential role of ANUSA in facilitating capacity building and fostering cooperation amongst governments, the scientific community and industry. For SKAO, these outcomes reaffirm the importance of sustained international cooperation across the scientific and commercial domains. As an intergovernmental research organization, we continue to work actively within the UN system, including through COPUOS and the ITU, along with industry and the broader astronomical community to support the need for coordinated mitigation efforts. The December workshop showcased that constructive, evidence-based dialogue remains essential for achieving the necessary balance between enabling innovation in satellite technologies and protecting major scientific infrastructures. Looking ahead, SKO is eager to build on the positive momentum generated by the workshop and therefore we are exploring the possibility of a moot court exercise focused on dark and quiet skies, which would be organised together with ANUSA and additional partners, tentatively envisaged for late 2027. This initiative would offer an innovative capacity building mechanism to help students, early career professionals and policymakers to engage directly with evolving legal questions related to satellite constellations, spectrum use and the preservation of astronomical environments. By fostering legal literacy and practical skills, such an initiative would complement ongoing technical work and strengthen the next generation of space law practitioners. Chair, distinguished delegates, the UN SKO workshop and its subsequent report demonstrates the continued importance of collective action to protect dark and quiet skies for the benefit of science and society. The Square Kilometre Array remains fully committed to supporting evidence-based policy makers, contributing technical expertise and expanding capacity building activities such as the proposed moot court. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with all member states and partners as COPUOS advances its critical work on these issues. I thank you, Chair.

I thank SKAO for that statement, and that is the last statement to be heard under agenda item four this morning. We will continue and hopefully conclude our consideration of this agenda item this afternoon. I would now like to continue and conclude our consideration of agenda item 12. In this context, I would like to give the floor to the first delegation on my list, which is the delegation of Indonesia.

Muchas gracias, señor Presidente. As a developing archipelagic nation increasingly reliant on space-based services, Indonesia views space traffic management as a critical element for the safe and sustainable use of outer space. Indonesia's growing space activities, ranging from small satellite development, earth observation missions, to national communication satellites, make it particularly vulnerable to congestion, collision risks, and the cascading efforts of space debris. At the same time, as a country with limited space infrastructure and technical resources compared to advanced space-faring nations, Indonesia has a strong interest in ensuring any space traffic management framework is inclusive, equitable, and accessible to all states. Indonesia recalls that the basic principles of international space law, including those in the Outer Space Treaty and related instruments, already provide a foundation for the peaceful and orderly use of outer space. However, the rapid growth of satellite constellations, more frequent launches, and increasing diversity of operators create new challenges. Indonesia therefore believes the legal aspects of space traffic management should be developed in a manner that reinforces the existing treaty frameworks, avoids exclusive zones or privileges that marginalize developing countries, and supports the long-term sustainability of outer space for all humanity. Indonesia also stresses that space traffic management should pay special attention to archipelagic and geographically dispersed states. These states depend on reliable satellite services for communication, maritime operations, and disaster management. Disruptions from collisions, debris, or opaque coordination practices could have serious consequences for such countries. Indonesia therefore advocates SDM arrangements that are transparent, non-discriminatory, equitably share burdens, including formation sharing mechanisms, and built on clear rules and procedures, emphasizing the need for capacity building for developing nations. We call for inclusive participation to ensure benefits are shared. Indonesia looks forward to contributing constructively to the development of legal approaches that serve the interest of all states, especially developing countries. Thank you.
I thank the delegation of Indonesia for that statement. I now give the floor to the delegation of Belgium.

Thank you, Chair, Chairperson, distinguished delegates. In recent years, space has become essential to many aspects of life on Earth. Technological progress and reduced costs have brought about fast growth, leading to increasing risks. The lack of space traffic coordination and management imperils not just the freedom of future generations to explore and use outer space. At a time when we increasingly depend on space technology on Earth, incidents in outer space can also imperil lives on Earth. Chairperson, Belgium welcomes the work carried out within the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, specifically the Working Group on the Long-Term Sustainability of Space Activities and its Group of Experts on Space Situational Awareness. Cooperation between the two subcommittees is crucial to moving forward on this matter, so as to offer an appropriate framework for discussions and to guarantee that the results can be used constructively. Consideration should be given to creating a specific working mechanism, such as a working group on the legal and policy aspects of space traffic. It is for this reason that, together with 16 other countries, Belgium co-sponsored Germany's initiative for a non-paper on assessing the legal and policy aspects of space traffic and forging consensus on the way forward. Chair, Belgium has integrated key principles on space traffic management into our space legislation. However, the initiatives undertaken by Belgium and several other countries, as well as existing international rules, remain insufficient in the absence of genuine common rules to coordinate and manage space traffic. A global approach is needed. Just like with airspace and high seas management, it's time to develop a straightforward and universal legal instrument establishing the rules of space navigation, including principles on minimum separation, priority and collision avoidance under appropriate international coordination. Such a framework should be based on enhanced space situational awareness capacity and on reliable mechanisms for data sharing while respecting security requirements and trust among operators. It must also encourage responsible conduct among operators, particularly when it comes to limiting space debris and the sustainability of space activities. Finally, above and beyond technical considerations, better space traffic coordination is also important for safety and stability and reduces the risk of misunderstandings among operators. The current risk level is too high to continue accepting the status quo. Thank you.
I thank the delegation of Belgium for that statement, and I now give the floor to the delegation of Japan.

Dear distinguished delegates, in outer space, the risk of collision between objects in Earth's orbit is steadily increasing due to the growing amount of space debris and the deployment of large-scale satellite constellations. Destructive actions such as anti-satellite tests have also spurred congestion. causing a growing threat to the sustainable and stable use of outer space. Japan attaches great importance to ensuring the safe, secure and sustainable use of outer space and encourages all states to advance space traffic management measures. Chairs, in line with our medium long term policy, which was revised in March 2026, Japan is advancing SSA and on orbit servicing initiatives, let me highlight some of our recent efforts, starting in 2026, Japan's Ministry of Defense and the self-defense Forces. will significantly expand their SSA capabilities, including upgrading the Space Operations Group to the Space Operations Corps and renaming the Air Self-Defense Force to the Aerospace Self-Defense Force as part of broader efforts to strengthen capabilities in the space domain. To ensure the safe, secure and transparent conduct on on orbit servicing, OOS, Japan established national guidelines in 2021, setting out key technical safety requirements. In line with these guidelines, JAXA is advancing RPO technology through the project called Commercial Removal of Debris demonstration in collaboration with a private company. Phase one was completed in 2024 and phase two is underway with a debris capture and removal demonstration plan for 2027. Japan encourages all relevant states to consider adapting national frameworks for the authorization of OOS activities, thereby contributing to the development of international norms and standards on safety and transparency. Chair, in February 2026, the Cabinet Office of Japan hosted the 11th International Symposium on Ensuring Safe and Sustainable Use of Outer Space, welcoming Ms. Arti Holamini, Director of UNOOSA, and other distinguished participants from government, academia, and industry. At the symposium, Japan shared its national efforts with the international community in order to promote transparency and cooperation of space activities. In conclusion, we'd like to reiterate Japan's commitment to contribute to international discussions on space traffic management to ensure the sustainable use of outer space for present and future generations.
Thank you very much to the delegation of Japan for that statement. And I now give the floor to the delegation of China.

Mr. Chair, currently the number of space objects has increased significantly with the global space congestion becoming increasingly severe and the risk of collision between space objects is growing exponentially. Mega satellite constellations are being deployed gradually and this has intensified congestion in low earth orbit. At the same time, large scale orbital maneuvers by mega constellations have made a space environment more complex. As a result, collision avoidance and space traffic management for spacecraft in orbit are facing unprecedented challenges. China welcomes the continued discussion at the legal committee. on the agenda item general exchange of views on legal space of space traffic management and wishes to express the following views. First, we must focus on international cooperation. Relevant discussions should contribute to strengthening international cooperation and information sharing, driving the international community to jointly address the proliferation of space debris and risk of spacecraft collision and other practical challenges in an effort to promote the safety and long-term sustainability of outer space activities. Second, we must fully consider the differences in space capability and technical levels of different countries. Space traffic management involves launch and different stages of outer space activities with numerous complex technical issues. countries have significant differences in their understanding and practices. Relevant discussions should avoid imposing excessive restrictions on exploration and use of outer space so that all countries, in particular developing countries and emerging space-faring nations have equal access to and use of outer space. Third, we must make full use of existing international space legal system. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, along with the Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines and the Guidelines for the Long-Term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities formulated by COPUOS provide specific guidance for debris prevention and control as well as end-of-life management for spacecraft. China calls on all countries to jointly maintain this existing governance system to ensure the orderly conduct of space activities and to promote the improvement of space traffic management. In recent years, China has actively taken a series of measures at domestic level and has explored ways to advance space traffic management. We would like to share our experience as follows. First, we formulated the administrative measures on the registration of space objects and the administrative measures on space debris mitigation. and prevention to regulate the domestic registration of space objects through a standardized system for space debris. Second, we have developed the specifications for space object orbital data and specifications for space object monitoring data among other national standards to provide clear guidance for objects requiring hazardous close approach assessment, collision avoidance, coordination and information notification. Third, we established a debris monitoring network. and an orbital database and a collision warning system to improve the situation awareness system and enhance the capability for safety management in orbit spacecraft. We have noticed that some delegations have once again noted the issue of the prohibition of direct ascent anti-satellite issues. This is under discussion in Geneva, and this is an arms control issue. We hope that discussions in Vienna will be more focused on the peaceful uses of outer space. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the delegation of China for that statement, and I now give the floor to the delegation of Saudi Arabia.

Excellency, Mr. Chair, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, in light of the rapid growth in the number of space objects, including satellites and space debris, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia would like to emphasize the importance of addressing the legal aspects related to space traffic coordination and space traffic management, in order to support the safety and sustainability of space operations. In this regard, the Kingdom confirms the importance of developing legal frameworks that support space traffic coordination and management, particularly in light of the rapid increase in the number of space objects and the associated notable rise in the likelihood of collisions and orbital maneuvers, which further highlights the need to develop such legal frameworks. Chair, the Kingdom considers that the main key enablers for space traffic management are the importance of national regulation and supervision of space object operations and control throughout the various phases of their journey, whether at launch, in orbit, or upon their return to Earth to achieve the peaceful, responsible, and sustainable use of outer space. The Kingdom also confirms the importance of developing technical capabilities related to space situational awareness given its key role in supporting space traffic management. Mr. Chair, in this context, the Kingdom is developing a national regulatory framework that includes the regulation of space object operations, space surveillance and tracking activities, as well as developing sustainability guidelines related to space activities in order to enable regulatory environment for space traffic management. The Kingdom is also working in cooperation with the private sector to develop infrastructure within the Kingdom for surveillance and tracking space objects in a manner that contributes to enhancing space situational awareness and supporting international efforts related to space traffic management. Mr. Chair, the Kingdom believes that the development of legal frameworks for space traffic management at the international level is a necessity in light of the rapid growth of the space objects, which requires work on an urgent track to develop legal frameworks for space traffic coordination alongside a comprehensive track to develop legal frameworks related to space traffic management. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the delegation of Saudi Arabia for that statement, and I now give the floor to the delegation of Brazil.

Thank you, Chair. Establishing clear and effective legal frameworks for space traffic management is a matter of the utmost importance for the future of space exploration and utilization. As access to space intensifies, it is urgent to develop a robust regulatory framework that ensures safety, sustainability, and international cooperation in the space environment. Proper space traffic management is not merely a matter of regulation and oversight. It is a global responsibility aimed at ensuring safe space operations, minimizing space debris, and ensuring that space activities are conducted in a sustainable manner. Chair. It is in the interest of the international community to make information on space situational awareness widely available to the extent possible and practicable. State and non-state actors must cooperate in the collection, validation, and sharing of data on orbital traffic, critical conjunctions, and space weather in order to ensure the safety of operations. In this context, It is essential to advance the development of a global database on space activities. Currently, collision avoidance measures and the sharing of orbital data rely primarily on voluntary initiatives and bilateral or regional arrangements, with no mandatory global framework in place. This gap can lead to fragmented approaches, especially given the growing diversity of space actors. There should be complementarity between the different SSA initiatives, both existing and planned, and not competition. In this context, Brazil advocates for the establishment of a clear international regulatory framework based on transparency and multilateral cooperation, which includes the definition of responsibilities, uniform technical criteria, and safeguards for data protection. Furthermore, we consider it important to encourage the creation of an international technical advisory body capable of advising space operators, recommending collision prevention measures and contributing to the development of common protocols and standards. Equally important is the strengthening of capacity building initiatives to enable developing countries to participate fully in future space traffic management systems. These include access to tracking data, the development of monitoring infrastructure, and the training of specialized personnel. The holding of the international symposium UN Space Sustainability, which took place in a hybrid format on January 2025, is particularly commendable. The event structured around practical workshops on space situational awareness and space traffic coordination demonstrated the importance of inclusive and accessible initiatives, enabling the participation of actors without prior technical training. Chair, the sustainability of space depends on adequate regulation of occupation and operation activities, as well as on mutual trust. In the light of the foregoing, Brazil reaffirms its commitment to the development of norms and mechanisms that promote a safer, more sustainable and more cooperative space environment in accordance with international law. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the delegation of Brazil for that statement and I now give the floor to the delegation of Colombia.

Thank you, Chair. To begin with, Colombia would like to commend the initiatives of the Study Group on Legal and Policy Aspects of Space Traffic Management and the Expert Group on Space Situational Awareness of the Working Group on Long-term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities. Given the growing complexity of the orbital environment, Colombia believes that it is crucial to make progress on strengthening the international legal framework on space traffic management. The increase in launches, ever denser orbits and the appearance of new space activities require mechanisms that guarantee the security, predictability and sustainability of outer space operations. Outer space is a common good, and therefore it requires shared commitments to protect it. In this regard, we support the creation of a broad international information system on space traffic, which includes better mechanisms for registry, notification protocols on launches, manoeuvres and re-entries, as well as technical and environmental provisions that will strengthen collective safety and security in outer space and space situational awareness. The system should be truly inclusive, accessible and non-discriminatory, ensuring that countries with emerging space-faring nations can participate on an equal footing and benefit from access to data and capacity. This, bearing in mind the accelerated increase in space traffic and the concentration of technological capacity in the hands of a few actors, which without specific measures could mean that systems for space traffic management would be designed and controlled principally by a very reduced small group. Therefore, it is urgent for the international community to adopt measures which ensure that the management of these activities do not increase existing gaps. Orbital saturation and the increase of objects in circulation do not just increase operational risks, they also limit the possibility of countries with lower capacity having access on an equitable and safe basis to the space environment. Therefore, there is a need for a collective effort focused on promoting responsible practices which allow for sustainable and more inclusive use of outer space. We would like to highlight that it is only through an inclusive legal architecture that it will be possible to build space governance that corresponds to the principles of cooperation, equitable access and common benefit for all humanity. We call for more robust multilateral agreements to be drawn up, particularly when it comes to defining standards and common principles for the management of space traffic. The architecture of space traffic management should not reproduce inequalities. On the contrary, it should guarantee shared benefits and effective participation of all States without leaving anybody behind.
I thank the delegation of Colombia for that statement and I now give the floor to the delegation of the Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Mr. Chair.

As we observe the recent surge in global space activities and ambitious goals of many nations, The Republic of Korea shares the growing concerns regarding the rapid congestion of outer space. This increasing density inevitably heightens the risk of orbital collisions, potential conflicts. The Republic of Korea believes that space traffic management is a critical agenda for ensuring the long-term safety and sustainability of space activities. Accordingly, we are actively engaged in international discussion on STM. Notably, in January of this year, we submitted our national response to UN OSA. Regarding the legal aspects of STM, at the national level, Korea continues to refine basis for the registration of space object and licensing region for space launch vehicles. Furthermore, our national plan for space as a preparedness identifies STM as a key emerging policy area, focusing on the advancement of relevant technologies and the strengthening of legal and institutional foundations. In line with this effort, Korea launched the development of the KSSA system this year. This AI based analytical platform with integrate multi source observational data from both ground and space basic ground and space based assets by analyzing potential collision risk and identifying of anomalous operation patterns. The KSSA system aims to enhance our timely decision making capabilities, thereby contributing to the space stripping risk mitigation. Mr. Chair, Recognizing the vital importance of STM, the Republic of Korea remains committed to international effort to establish global standards. We look forward to playing a continuous and constructive role in the development of a global STM framework.

Thank you.
I thank the delegation of the Republic of Korea for that statement, and now I give the floor to the delegation of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for giving me the floor. My delegation recalls that the issue of space traffic management is intrinsically linked to the principle of freedom of exploration and use of outer space, as enshrined in the Outer Space Treaty. This freedom is not without limits. It's accompanied by the obligations of due regard, cooperation, and mutual assistance. Taken together, these principles require us to coordinate space activities in a manner that ensures that outer space remains safe, sustainable and accessible to all. However, the current lack of comprehensive rules for the coordination, and even more so the management, of space traffic is a matter of growing concern. This subcommittee should therefore devote focused attention to this issue. In this regard, my delegation welcomes the working paper entitled Assessing Legal and Policy Aspects of Space Traffic and Forging Consensus on the Way Forward presented under the leadership of Germany. We are pleased to co-sponsor this initiative. The paper provides a valuable overview of existing national regulations, policies, best practices and requirements and identifies areas of convergence that can guide our future work. In particular, it highlights the growing development of national frameworks, the importance of transparency and information sharing, and the relevance of existing international norms. We would support the proposal raised by our German colleagues to consider continuing this work through a dedicated working group under this agenda item. Such a mechanism could allow for structured exchanges and contribute to the gradual development of common approaches while remaining complementary to the work of the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, including the Working Group on the Long-Term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities and the Expert Group on Space Situational Awareness. Together, the technical and legal tracks could lead to concrete outcomes within the committee as a whole. Finally, Mr. Chair, my delegation stresses the urgency of this matter. Just as air traffic relies on coordination to ensure safety, so too must space activities. Without effective space traffic management, and given the worrying developments regarding space debris as previously discussed, the risk of collisions and disruption will continue to grow. This threatens not only the sustainability of the space environment but also the critical services upon which our societies on earth increasingly depend. I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank the delegation of the Netherlands for that statement and I now give the floor to the delegation of France.

Thank you Chairperson, distinguished delegates. For more than 30 years now, France has had in place a coherent national program for space traffic, which was enshrined as a top priority in our national space strategy. The program has two pillars. Firstly, an operational and capacity pillar. Coordinating space traffic means having space situational awareness and monitoring capacity. This is crucial to eliminating collision risk. For that purpose, France is one of the main contributors to the EU SST partnership funded by the EU. Space situational awareness capacity should also be flanked by innovative technology from the private sector. In the interest of a global approach and in view of the swift increase in space traffic, France supports the creation of a space monitoring surveillance mechanism that would allow the sharing and updating of operational contact points among satellite operators. To that end, we encourage the continued pursuit of the work of the SSA group of experts chaired by UAE. The second pillar is regulatory. An international incremental approach needs to be pursued based on the adoption of guidelines allowing rapid and tangible progress. Uh, the progressive crafting of such standards applied reciprocally should allow the resolution of immediate operational challenges and also allow to establish an inclusive, uh, consensus that takes aboard the perspective of effective private sector actors. France therefore supports Germany's CRP aimed at coordinating national legal practices as regards space traffic. France has adopted an innovative regulatory framework that meets space traffic management challenges and requires operators to have anti-collision operational capacity. It also strengthens space object identification and monitoring and restricts access to certain orbits for non-maneuvering objects and limits the residual duration of short missions. The legal framework applies also to constellations and in-orbit services. At the European level, France welcomes the progress in the EU Space Act, strengthening safety, resilience and sustainability in space, which will facilitate enhanced space traffic management. Chair, the success of the efforts to secure comprehensive governance of space traffic management depends on it being accompanied by operational coordination of space traffic. Thank you.
I thank the delegation of France for that statement and I now give the floor to the delegation of Slovenia.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, distinguished delegates. Slovenia welcomed that COPUOS requested UNOOSA to collect information on the relevant regulation, policies and requirements regarding space traffic management from all member states and permanent observers. We have long recognized space traffic management as one of the most urgent and strategically important challenges facing the international space community. In our view, it is only through an effective space traffic system that we can assure that our space systems remain protected and operational. In light of this, we again welcome the establishment of the expert group on the space situational awareness and thank the United Arab Emirates for their able leadership. Yet besides technical aspects of space traffic, we firmly believe that this subcommittee is required to focus on the legal and policy aspects of space traffic, in particular the governance, use and sharing of technical and operational information in effective space situational awareness. We fully support the German proposal and their conference room paper on the legal aspects of space traffic management. In particular, we are of the view that the ongoing work within the scientific and technical subcommittee, including the activities of the working group on the long-term sustainability of outer space activities and its expert group on space situational awareness, would be complemented by the work done in this subcommittee and would potentially lead to more solutions in a timely manner. We would especially like to commend the proposal to consider the establishment of a dedicated working group on the legal and policy aspects of space traffic management. Slovenia strongly supports this initiative. It is time to move beyond general discussions and towards the substantive and meaningful discussions about concrete, actionable outcomes that address the legal dimensions of the SDM. Slovenia actively supported and promoted a European approach to space traffic management. A key milestone in this process was the European Space Traffic Management Conference entitled Fostering a European Approach on Space Traffic Management, which was held on 7th of July, 2021 in a virtual format, which brought together EU member states, the European Space Agency and EU institutions. The strong participation highlighted a shared recognition of the importance of STM and the need for collective European action. Five years since the organization of this event is a significant milestone and therefore Slovenia, in collaboration with the European Commission, decided to organize the follow up event in Slovenia this September. In conclusion, Slovenia reaffirms its belief that SDM is not merely a technical issue. It is a matter of responsible governance, international cooperation and collective protection of a domain that is essential for scientific progress, economic development and global security. I thank you, Mr. Chair, and distinguished delegates for your kind attention.
I thank the delegation of Slovenia for that statement and I now give the floor to the delegation of New Zealand.

New Zealand believes that work under this agenda item should prioritise three areas: the effective use of current non-binding instruments, the role of commercial and non-government institutions in space traffic management, and practical actions to advance a common understanding of space traffic management. Transparency, timely communication, and information sharing under the Registration Convention remain fundamental to effective international coordination of space traffic. The increasing congestion in Earth orbits and the rise in conjunction alerts demonstrate that space traffic management, STM, is no longer a theoretical concept, but an operational necessity. Although the term STM does not explicitly appear in existing treaties, its legal foundations are firmly anchored in the OST 1967, particularly Article 6, which mandates authorisation and continuing supervision, and Article 9, which requires due regard to avoid interference with other States' activities. These principles are operationalised through national regulatory measures, including the Malaysian Space Board Act 2022, and must be complemented by standardised coordination and transparency at the international level. Mr. Cheng, Malaysia wishes to highlight three key considerations. First, STM is a shared responsibility. All states depend on orbital sustainability for critical services such as navigation and disaster response. Therefore, operators must have reliable access to space situational awareness, SSA, and structured traffic coordination mechanisms to ensure safety. Second, Malaysia's own experience with a near-miss conjunction event in 2025 reinforced the immediate nature of orbital risks. This incident highlighted the critical importance of integrating SSA considerations into national authorisation and continuing supervision frameworks under the Malaysian Space Board Act 2022. It also underscored the urgent need for reliable, timely and transparent communication channels among satellite operators globally to uphold the principle of due regard under Article 9. And third, Malaysia believes that UN COPUOS must lead in ensuring that STM governance remains multilateral, inclusive and consistent with the OST 1967. A coordinated international approach is essential. to operationalise Article 9 and support States in fulfilling Article 6 for authorisation and supervision. Chair, presently a legal or regulatory definition of a small satellite does not exist. And under the United Nations treaties, principles and resolutions relating to international space law, the term space object refers to satellites, launch vehicles, and their component parts. Considering the essential roles of space objects, regardless of their size, in the socio-economic development of Member States, the Group is of the view that the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and its subcommittees should not impose any limitations on designing, building, launching and use of space objects by developing countries. The Group also reiterates its previous statements regarding, one, the importance of ensuring guaranteed and equitable access to orbital positions of the geostationary orbit according to the needs of all countries, in particular developing countries. Two, that no space object should be removed or eliminated without prior consent or authorization of the registering state. And three, since debris generation goes against the interest of all states, satellite removal or elimination should be done in a responsible manner. Thank you, Chair.
